_purpose: S53 (Session 70): an index of the 17 designs' and mechanisms' own primary sources, for the blind re-read of C2.6, C3.6 and C4.6 in Session 76 (S59). Session 65 scored all 17 at 0.5 on a stated rule without reading these sources (NEEC_Rescoring_s65.md, line 1492: 'the least-read units in the pass'). This file names, for each unit, the authoritative text(s) describing its own governance/consent provisions (C2.6), its productivity and investment-allocation mechanism (C3.6), and its harm-liability and regulatory provisions (C4.6), plus any existing in-repo passage already touching one of these three. It does not read or score any unit; a citation marked 'cached' is in evidence_cache/ by file name, one marked 'cite only' is not fetched this session (see note).
note: Ten of the 17 (MS, LM, MMT, UBI, DG, SC, FALC, PE, CCO, INT) predate the scratch-file format and are either one-line entries in NEEC_Report_v1_6.md or (INT only) have an external white paper already cached. Seven (GEO, MC, DE, UBS, SWF, IF, OS) have a dedicated scoring scratch file in the repository, written before v2.0 added C2.6/C3.6/C4.6; grepping each for governance/consent/liability/productivity keywords found only 0-12 hits apiece (recorded below), confirming these files do not substantively cover the three new criteria either. For 16 of the 17 the primary design literature is commercially published (books) or, for CCO, a separate repository (BetterToBest/compassionism-simulation); this session cites each by author/title/year/edition rather than bulk-downloading copyrighted text, consistent with the scratch files' own practice of quoting short passages rather than storing whole works. Session 76 should fetch the specific pages a library, archive.org borrowing, or the design's own excerpt permits, and quote under the same short-passage practice the existing scratch files use.

MS.home_document: NEEC_Report_v1_6.md (one-line entries only; no scratch file)
primary_sources: John E. Roemer, A Future for Socialism (Harvard University Press, 1994) -- ch. 1-5 on worker/public ownership and market allocation bear on C3.6's investment mechanism; ch. 6-7 on the coupon economy's institutions bear on C2.6's governance/due-process questions.

David Schweickart, After Capitalism, 2nd ed. (Rowman & Littlefield, 2011) -- pt. II on 'Economic Democracy' describes the worker-council governance structure (C2.6) and the public investment bank mechanism (C3.6).

Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (Basic Books, 1974) -- pt. I (ch. 3-5) on the minimal state's protective function and due process bears on C2.6; the book has no developed productivity or harm-liability mechanism beyond tort law under common law, so C3.6 and C4.6 clause 2 may be 'not shown' on this source alone.
L. Randall Wray, Modern Money Theory, 2nd ed. (Palgrave Macmillan, 2015) -- ch. 1-2 on sovereign currency issuance bear on C3.6 (demand management, not an investment-allocation mechanism as such).

Pavlina R. Tcherneva, The Case for a Job Guarantee (Polity, 2020) -- freely summarized in her Levy Institute working papers (levyinstitute.org, reachable this session); the job guarantee's administration (local hiring boards, wage floor) bears on C2.6's due-process question and C4.6's regulatory-capture question (public employment, not a private regulator).

Philippe Van Parijs and Yannick Vanderborght, Basic Income: A Radical Proposal for a Free Society and a Sane Economy (Harvard University Press, 2017) -- ch. 1 and 9 on UBI as an unconditional transfer bear on C2.6 (no conditionality to police) but the book proposes no productivity or harm-liability mechanism of its own; C3.6 and C4.6 read on the host economy (protocol 3.2), as C1.4 and C4.5 already do for this unit.
Jason Hickel, Less Is More: How Degrowth Will Save the World (Windmill Books, 2020) -- ch. 6 ('Post-Capitalism') on worker cooperatives and public ownership bears on C2.6 and C3.6.

Giorgos Kallis et al., The Case for Degrowth (Polity, 2020) -- ch. 3 on redistribution and democratic planning bears on C2.6; the book explicitly rejects productivity growth as a goal (C3.6's clauses 1-2 may be 'out of reach' by the design's own statement, as C4.2 already found for growth).

Klaus Schwab with Peter Vanham, Stakeholder Capitalism: A Global Economy that Works for Progress, People and Planet (Wiley, 2021) -- ch. 8 ('A New Social Contract') and the World Economic Forum's 'Davos Manifesto 2020' (weforum.org, freely published) bear on C2.6 (stated governance commitments) and C4.6 (stated harm-disclosure commitments); the design states no liability-enforcement mechanism of its own, only voluntary ESG reporting.

Aaron Bastani, Fully Automated Luxury Communism (Verso, 2019) -- ch. 8 ('Four Futures, or Communism') describes common ownership of automated production (C3.6's investment-allocation question) but states no court, regulator or due-process institution (C2.6, C4.6 clause 2 likely 'not shown').

Michael Albert and Robin Hahnel, Looking Forward: Participatory Economics for the Twenty First Century (South End Press, 1991; a later restatement is Albert, Parecon: Life After Capitalism, Verso, 2003) -- the 'participatory planning' procedure (ch. 4-5 of Looking Forward) is parecon's investment-allocation mechanism (C3.6); the workers'- and consumers'-council structure and its grievance procedure bear on C2.6. participatoryeconomics.info (reachable this session) hosts summaries and may host excerpts; full chapters were not located as free full text this session.

DE.home_document: NEEC_DoughnutEconomics_scoring_scratch.md (grep: 3 hits on governance/regulation/productivity keywords, none on the C2.6/C4.6 clauses as v2.0 states them)

primary_sources: Thomas H. primary_sources: Elinor Ostrom, Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action (Cambridge University Press, 1990) -- ch. 3's eight 'design principles' (graduated sanctions, conflict-resolution mechanisms, recognized rights to organize) are precisely C2.6's governance question; ch. 3-5's monitoring and sanctioning systems bear on C4.6 clause 2 (who enforces harm rules and how); the book is not public domain and was not fetched this session.

Elinor Ostrom, 'Collective Action and the Evolution of Social Norms', Journal of Economic Perspectives 14(3) (2000) -- freely available via JSTOR/the author's university page in some instances; not confirmed reachable this session.
